outline.chapter_title: FOIA’s Disclosure Mandate and the Exemption 7(A) Framework
outline.description: This chapter introduces the statutory framework that controls the case: FOIA’s general rule of disclosure, Exemption 7(A)’s protection for certain law-enforcement records, and FOIA’s independent segregability requirement. It gives the legal vocabulary needed to understand the dispute before turning to the facts.
subtopics: FOIA’s basic obligation to disclose agency records unless a statutory exemption applies
The text of Exemption 7(A): records compiled for law enforcement purposes whose disclosure could reasonably be expected to interfere with enforcement proceedings
The D.C. Circuit’s gloss that the relevant enforcement proceedings must be pending or reasonably anticipated
Why ongoing criminal investigations can qualify as enforcement proceedings
FOIA’s segregability rule and the duty to release reasonably segregable nonexempt information
How category-based withholding and agency declarations function in FOIA litigation
The special role of deference when the FBI invokes Exemption 7(A), especially in national-security and counterterrorism contexts

outline.chapter_title: Farahi’s FBI File Request and the Long Path to Appeal
outline.description: This chapter sets out the factual and procedural history that generated the appeal. It explains Farahi’s immigration-related background, the scope of his FOIA request, the FBI’s staged processing of responsive material, and the district court’s two-step handling of summary judgment.
subtopics: Farahi’s background as an Iranian national living in the United States and his placement in removal proceedings
The role of terrorism-related allegations in Farahi’s immigration proceedings
Farahi’s FOIA request for his FBI file and the breadth of potentially responsive material: thousands of pages and dozens of CDs
The FBI’s delayed response, partial disclosures, and extensive withholdings
The FBI’s first summary-judgment motion supported by David Hardy’s public declaration and sealed ex parte supplement
The district court’s 2022 ruling: provisional acceptance of Exemption 7(A), concern about staleness, and request for updated submissions
The FBI’s renewed motion supported by Joseph Bender’s public and ex parte declarations
The district court’s final grant of summary judgment and Farahi’s appeal

outline.chapter_title: Appellate Review and the First Exemption 7(A) Requirement: Records Compiled for Law Enforcement Purposes
outline.description: This chapter explains the standard of review and then analyzes the first substantive element of Exemption 7(A). It shows how the court assessed whether the FBI adequately connected Farahi’s file to legitimate law-enforcement and national-security investigations.
subtopics: De novo appellate review of summary judgment in FOIA cases
The government’s burden to justify withholding under a FOIA exemption
The FBI’s law-enforcement status and the resulting measure of judicial deference
The Pratt/Campbell nexus requirement: tying the investigation to an FBI law-enforcement duty and a possible security risk or violation of law
What the Hardy declarations said about investigations involving national security, international terrorism, and related proceedings
How Farahi’s own concessions in district court reinforced the law-enforcement character of the file
Why the court found no serious doubt that the records were compiled for law-enforcement purposes

outline.chapter_title: The Second Exemption 7(A) Requirement: Interference with Pending or Reasonably Anticipated Proceedings
outline.description: This chapter covers the core dispute on appeal: whether disclosure could reasonably be expected to interfere with enforcement proceedings that still existed when the district court ruled. It explains the court’s treatment of passage of time, the interaction between the Hardy and Bender declarations, and the forfeited challenge to the FBI’s document categories.
subtopics: The interference requirement and the need for a concrete pending or reasonably anticipated proceeding
Accepted Exemption 7(A) rationale: disclosure could tip off targets to the scope and direction of an investigation
The Hardy declaration’s statement that the investigation was ongoing and the importance of the ex parte details
Why the Bender declaration was viewed as an update confirming continuity rather than a standalone justification
Farahi’s reliance on CREW and his argument that the updated declaration was too conclusory
The court’s response to staleness concerns and its emphasis on procedural context
How the breadth and seriousness of the publicly described counterterrorism investigation supported the FBI’s position
The holding that the FBI showed a continuing concrete prospective law-enforcement proceeding
Farahi’s challenge to the FBI’s withholding categories and why the court deemed that argument forfeited for lack of specificity

outline.chapter_title: Segregability, Ex Parte Submissions, and the Case’s Final Significance
outline.description: This chapter explains why the court still required a separate segregability analysis even after finding Exemption 7(A) applicable, why it accepted the FBI’s ex parte showing, and how these conclusions led to affirmance. It closes by identifying the opinion’s practical significance for FOIA cases involving ongoing national-security investigations.
subtopics: FOIA’s independent requirement to segregate and release nonexempt information whenever reasonably possible
The district court’s concern that the initial record was insufficient on segregability
Bender’s supplemental ex parte explanation for why exempt and nonexempt material was not meaningfully separable
The Mead Data principle that scattered words or phrases need not be released when no meaningful information can be segregated
Why the court rejected Farahi’s intuition that the sheer volume of records must contain releasable material
The permissibility of relying on ex parte declarations when public explanation would reveal the very information at stake
Farahi’s failure to preserve an objection to the use of ex parte submissions
The final disposition: affirmance of summary judgment for the FBI
What the opinion illustrates about updated agency declarations, judicial deference, and FOIA litigation over active counterterrorism files
